question: What is a Standard Instrument Departure (SID)?

options.text: A published route connecting the departure runway to the en-route structure, designed for obstacle clearance and traffic flow
A visual-only departure procedure
A holding procedure flown immediately after takeoff
The clearance limit assigned to a flight

explanation: A SID is a published departure procedure designed to take an aircraft from the runway to the en-route phase while ensuring obstacle clearance and fitting into the surrounding traffic flow.

question: What is a Standard Terminal Arrival Route (STAR)?

options.text: A published route linking the en-route structure to an initial approach fix or a transition near the destination
A departure procedure flown from the runway
A missed approach procedure
An emergency descent procedure

explanation: A STAR bridges the en-route phase and the approach phase, taking traffic from the en-route structure down to a point where an instrument approach can begin.

question: What is the purpose of naming an alternate aerodrome on an IFR flight plan?

options.text: It has no operational purpose and is purely administrative
To provide a planned aerodrome the flight can safely divert to if the intended destination cannot be used, for example due to weather below applicable minima
It is only ever required for VFR flights
It replaces the requirement to carry fuel reserves

explanation: An alternate gives the flight a planned, fuel-accounted-for option if the destination becomes unusable; it does not remove the separate requirement to carry reserve fuel.

question: What does a "clearance limit" define?

options.text: The maximum altitude ATC will ever assign to an aircraft
The point to which an ATC clearance is valid — the aircraft is not authorised to proceed beyond it without a further clearance
The last waypoint published on every SID
The runway assigned for landing

explanation: The clearance limit is the fix, point or aerodrome beyond which the aircraft must not proceed without receiving a further clearance from ATC.

question: On an IFR en-route chart, what does a published airway with a stated MEA typically represent?

options.text: A route with no associated navigation aids at all
An established route between defined fixes or navigation aids, published with a minimum altitude that meets obstacle clearance and signal coverage requirements
A corridor reserved for VFR traffic only
The boundary of a prohibited area

explanation: An airway is a defined, charted route between fixes or navigation aids, published together with its minimum en-route altitude so pilots and ATC share the same reference for that segment.

question: What does the term "squawk" refer to in IFR operations?

options.text: A radio call used to request a weather update
Setting the transponder to the code ATC has assigned, so the aircraft can be identified on radar
A specific type of holding pattern
A report filed after a missed approach

explanation: "Squawk" instructs the pilot to set a specific transponder code, which lets ATC's radar systems positively identify and track that aircraft.

question: Why are instrument charts (departure, arrival and approach) revised and re-published on a regular cycle?

options.text: To reflect changes to procedures, obstacles, navigation aids or minima, so pilots always fly with current and accurate data
Purely for cosmetic or formatting reasons
Charts are not revised once first published
Only to change the paper size used for printing

explanation: Airspace, obstacles, equipment and procedures change over time; a regular revision cycle (such as an AIRAC cycle) keeps published data — and the minima and paths pilots rely on — current.
